kangaroo-at-2019-student-01.title: Compare the rectangles
kangaroo-at-2019-student-01.body:
The three rectangles are congruent. The dark one on the left is a full-height strip; the white one is half the height of the flag.

Let the white rectangle have height $x$ and width $y$. The dark rectangle has height $2x$ (the full flag height). Being congruent to the white one, its sides are also $x$ and $y$; its height $2x$ is not $x$, so $y=2x$.

So the white rectangle has sides $x$ and $2x$: ratio $1:2$.

**Answer: (A) 1 : 2**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-01.title: Measure the flag
kangaroo-at-2019-student-01.body:
Let the flag be $W$ wide and $H$ high. The dark strip is $\frac W3\times H$ (one third of the area), the white rectangle is $\frac{2W}3\times\frac H2$. Congruent means $\frac W3=\frac H2$ and $H = \frac{2W}{3}$ — the same condition. Then the white rectangle is $\frac{2W}3\times\frac W3$, ratio $1:2$.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-02.title: Total of 10
kangaroo-at-2019-student-02.body:
The two row sums add up to $1+2+3+4=10$, and so do the two column sums.

4 and 5 cannot both be row sums (or both column sums), since $4+5\ne10$. So one of them is a row sum and the other a column sum. The other row/column sums are then $10-4=6$ and $10-5=5$.

**Answer: (E) 5 and 6**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-02.title: Example
kangaroo-at-2019-student-02.body:
Table $\begin{array}{cc}1&3\\4&2\end{array}$: rows 4 and 6, columns 5 and 5. Indeed the remaining sums are 5 and 6.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-03.title: Half of each strip
kangaroo-at-2019-student-03.body:
A triangle whose base is one side of a rectangular strip and whose apex is on the opposite side covers exactly half of that strip.

In (A), (B), (C) and (D) the grey parts are such triangles (in (A) and (B) the grey and white triangles are mirror images), so in each of these pictures exactly half of the rectangle is grey.

In (E) three strips are half grey, but one strip is completely grey, so more than half is grey.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-04.title: Check each pair
kangaroo-at-2019-student-04.body:
Look at the triangles in pairs and note, at each crossing, which triangle lies on top.

In the original picture the grey and the white triangle are hooked into each other (each one passes once over and once under the other), the white and the black triangle are hooked into each other as well, and the grey and the black triangle are not hooked at all.

In (B) and (C) the colours are arranged differently (another triangle is in the middle). Comparing the crossings of (A), (D) and (E) with the original, only in (D) the grey triangle is hooked into the white one, the white into the black, and the grey and black ones merely lie on top of each other without being linked.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-05.title: Base and sides
kangaroo-at-2019-student-05.body:
The triangular faces are the side faces, one for each side of the base. So the base is a 23-gon. The pyramid has 23 base edges and 23 edges going up to the apex: $46$ edges.

**Answer: (C) 46**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-06.title: Write the sum
kangaroo-at-2019-student-06.body:
The numbers are $7243$, $21x7$ and $yz26$ (hidden digits $x$, $y$, $z$). Then
$$7243 + 21x7 + yz26 = 11126.$$
With the hidden digits 0 the sum would be $7243+2107+26 = 9376$; the missing $11126-9376 = 1750 = 1000y + 100z + 10x$. So $y=1$, $z=7$, $x=5$.

Hidden digits: 1, 5 and 7.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-06.title: Column by column
kangaroo-at-2019-student-06.body:
Units: $3+7+6=16$, write 6 carry 1 ✓. Tens: $4+x+2+1$ ends in 2, so $x=5$ (sum 12, carry 1). Hundreds: $2+1+z+1$ ends in 1, so $z=7$ (sum 11, carry 1). Thousands: $7+2+y+1 = 11$ gives $y=1$.

**Answer: (B) 1, 5 and 7**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-07.title: Fewest digits
kangaroo-at-2019-student-07.body:
The smallest number has as few digits as possible, so we use as many 9s as possible: $2019 = 9\cdot224+3$, so we need at least 225 digits. Among 225-digit numbers with digit sum 2019 the smallest puts the small digit in front: $3\underbrace{99\ldots9}_{224}$.

The first digit is **3**.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-08.title: Multiples
kangaroo-at-2019-student-08.body:
The multiples of $2^{10}$ in this range are $k\cdot 2^{10}$ with $2^{10}\le k\cdot2^{10}\le 2^{13}=8\cdot2^{10}$, i.e. $k=1,2,\dots,8$. That is **8** numbers.

**Answer: (D) 8**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-09.title: Count the faces
kangaroo-at-2019-student-09.body:
With 6 faces the probabilities mean: 3 faces show one dot, 2 faces show two dots and only **1** face shows three dots.

Picture (C) shows two different faces with three dots each, which is impossible. The other pictures show at most one face with three dots, at most two faces with two dots and at most three with one dot.

**Answer: (C)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-10.title: Contrapositive
kangaroo-at-2019-student-10.body:
"If Bob has no hat, Carl has a hat." Carl has no hat, so Bob must have a hat (otherwise Carl would wear one).

About Alex we learn nothing: the first rule only says something when Alex has no hat, and Bob wears a hat either way. Both "Alex with hat" and "Alex without hat" are consistent.

So for sure only **Bob** wears a hat.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-11.title: Factor out 7!
kangaroo-at-2019-student-11.body:
$$7!+8!+9! = 7!\,(1+8+8\cdot9) = 7!\cdot81 = 7!\cdot3^4.$$
$7! = 5040 = 2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7$ contains $3^2$. So the number contains exactly $3^{2+4}=3^6$.

**Answer: (D) $3^6$**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-12.title: Set up
kangaroo-at-2019-student-12.body:
Last year: $b$ boys and $g$ girls. Now $1.2b + 0.8g = b+g+1$, so $0.2b-0.2g=1$, i.e. $b=g+5$.

For $20\%$ of $b$ and of $g$ to be whole numbers, $b$ and $g$ must be multiples of 5. Now there are $1.2(g+5)+0.8g = 2g+6$ students, with $g = 0, 5, 10, \dots$: $6, 16, 26, 36, \dots$.

Of the options only $26$ works ($g=10$, $b=15$: now 18 boys and 8 girls).

**Answer: (B) 26**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-12.title: Think in changes
kangaroo-at-2019-student-12.body:
The boys gained $\frac15$ of their number, the girls lost $\frac15$ of theirs, and the net change is $+1$: so the boys' gain exceeds the girls' loss by 1. With $b=5m$, $g=5k$ the change is $m-k=1$. The new total is $6m+4k = 6(k+1)+4k = 10k+6$, which ends in 6: only 26.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-13.title: Base areas
kangaroo-at-2019-student-13.body:
Let the edges be $x,y,z$. Standing on the different faces, the water volume is base area × depth:
$$yz\cdot2 = xz\cdot3 = xy\cdot5 = 120,$$
so $yz=60$, $xz=40$, $xy=24$. Multiplying: $(xyz)^2 = 60\cdot40\cdot24 = 57600$, so $xyz = 240$.

**Answer: (E) 240 m³**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-14.title: Expand both sides
kangaroo-at-2019-student-14.body:
$(a\diamond b)\diamond c = c-(b-a) = c-b+a$.

$a\diamond(b\diamond c) = (c-b)-a = c-b-a$.

Equal means $a=-a$, i.e. $a=0$ (and $b,c$ arbitrary).

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-15.title: Halving twice
kangaroo-at-2019-student-15.body:
Rope 1 runs from P over the fixed pulley, down around the middle pulley and up to the ceiling. Pulling out 24 cm of rope at P shortens the two strands holding the middle pulley by 24 cm in total, so the middle pulley rises $12$ cm.

Rope 2 hangs from the middle pulley, runs around the lower pulley Q and up to the ceiling. The middle pulley rising 12 cm frees 12 cm of rope 2, shared by the two strands holding Q, so Q rises $6$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 6**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-16.title: Use the smallest prime factor
kangaroo-at-2019-student-16.body:
The biggest proper factor of $n$ is $\frac np$, where $p$ is the smallest prime factor of $n$ (for $n$ prime, $\frac np = 1$). So we need
$$n-\frac np = 6 \iff n = \frac{6p}{p-1}.$$
Since $p-1$ and $p$ have no common factor, $p-1$ must divide 6: $p\in\{2,3,4,7\}$, and $p$ prime leaves $p=2,3,7$, giving $n=12, 9, 7$.

Check: $12$: smallest prime 2, biggest factor $6=12-6$ ✓. $9$: biggest factor $3 = 9-6$ ✓. $7$: biggest factor $1=7-6$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-17.title: Position of the sweet
kangaroo-at-2019-student-17.body:
Imagine all five balls being drawn in order. The boiled sweet is equally likely to be in each of the 5 positions. Maria draws positions 2 and 4, so she wins with probability $\frac25$.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-17.title: Step by step
kangaroo-at-2019-student-17.body:
Maria wins on draw 2: $\frac45\cdot\frac14=\frac15$. On draw 4: $\frac45\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac12=\frac15$. Total $\frac25$.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-18.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2019-student-18.body:
Put the bottom-left corner of the small square at the origin. The grey triangle has vertices $(0,0)$, $(a,a)$ (top right of the small square) and $(a+b,b)$ (top right of the big square). Its area is
$$\tfrac12\,|a\cdot b - a\cdot(a+b)| = \tfrac12a^2.$$

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-18.title: Base times height
kangaroo-at-2019-student-18.body:
Put the bottom-left corner of the small square at $O=(0,0)$. The grey triangle is $O$, $P=(a,a)$, $R=(a+b,b)$. The side $OR$ lies on the line $y=\frac{b}{a+b}x$. Above $x=a$ this line has height $\frac{ab}{a+b}$, so the vertical segment from $P$ down to $OR$ has length $a-\frac{ab}{a+b}=\frac{a^2}{a+b}$.

This vertical segment splits the triangle into two triangles with total "width" $a+b$, so the area is $\frac12\cdot\frac{a^2}{a+b}\cdot(a+b)=\frac12a^2$.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-19.title: Squeeze between 4 and 5
kangaroo-at-2019-student-19.body:
If $0<x<5$ then $\sqrt{20+x}<\sqrt{25}=5$, and $\sqrt{20+x}>\sqrt{20}>4$.

Starting with $\sqrt{20}$, which lies between 4 and 5, every further step $x\mapsto\sqrt{20+x}$ keeps the value between 4 and 5. So the whole expression is between 4 and 5, and the biggest integer below it is **4**.

**Answer: (A) 4**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-20.title: Count the shared vertices twice
kangaroo-at-2019-student-20.body:
There are three squares; two vertices $x$ and $y$ are shared by neighbouring squares. Adding the three square sums counts every number once and $x$, $y$ twice:
$$3S = 55 + x + y.$$
Since $x+y\ge 1+2=3$, $3S\ge58$, so $S\ge20$ (as $S$ is an integer).

$S=20$ is possible: shared vertices $1$ and $4$, left square $1,2,8,9$, middle square $1,4,5,10$, right square $4,3,6,7$ — each sum is 20.

**Answer: (C) 20**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-22.title: Split by sign
kangaroo-at-2019-student-22.body:
- $x\ge0$: $2-x=ax$, so $x=\frac2{1+a}$, which is a valid (positive) solution exactly when $a>-1$.
- $x<0$: $2+x=ax$, so $x=\frac2{a-1}$, valid (negative) exactly when $a<1$.

Two solutions exactly when both hold: $-1<a<1$, i.e. $a\in\,]-1;1[$.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-22.title: Graphs
kangaroo-at-2019-student-22.body:
$y=2-|x|$ is a tent with slopes $+1$ and $-1$ and apex $(0,2)$; $y=ax$ is a line through the origin, below the apex. It meets the right arm iff it is not parallel to it or steeper downwards, i.e. $a>-1$, and the left arm iff $a<1$. Both: $-1<a<1$.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-23.title: Add the two equations
kangaroo-at-2019-student-23.body:
$a+\frac bc = 11$ and $b+\frac ac=14$. Adding: $(a+b)\left(1+\frac1c\right)=25$, so with $k=\frac{a+b}c$:
$$k(c+1) = 25.$$
Also $a+b = kc$. Since $c\ge1$, $c+1\in\{5,25\}$.

- $c=4$, $k=5$: $a+b=20$ and subtracting the equations, $(b-a)(1-\frac14)=3$, $b-a=4$: $a=8$, $b=12$. Check: $8+3=11$, $12+2=14$ ✓.
- $c=24$, $k=1$: $(b-a)\cdot\frac{23}{24}=3$ has no integer solution.

So $\frac{a+b}c=5$.

**Answer: (E) 5**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-24.title: Classify the planes
kangaroo-at-2019-student-24.body:
Any three vertices determine a plane; group the planes by how many vertices they contain.

- The 6 **faces** (4 vertices each).
- The 6 **diagonal rectangles** through two opposite edges (4 vertices each).
- Planes with exactly 3 vertices: cutting off one corner, through the three neighbours of a vertex — one for each of the 8 vertices.

Any three vertices lie in one of these (if two of them are on a common edge or face diagonal, check that the plane is a face or diagonal rectangle; otherwise they are the three neighbours of a vertex). Total $6+6+8 = 20$.

**Answer: (E) 20**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-24.title: Count triples
kangaroo-at-2019-student-24.body:
There are $\binom83=56$ triples of vertices. Each 4-vertex plane contains $\binom43=4$ triples, each 3-vertex plane contains 1. With 12 four-vertex planes: $56-12\cdot4 = 8$ triples left, giving 8 more planes. Total $12+8=20$.

**Answer: (E) 20**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-25.title: Vieta for each line
kangaroo-at-2019-student-25.body:
A vertical line $x=0$ meets the parabola only once, so all four lines have the form $y=kx$. Intersection: $x^2-2=kx$, i.e. $x^2-kx-2=0$, which always has two real roots with product $-2$ (Vieta).

The product of all eight x-coordinates is $(-2)^4 = 16$, whatever the lines are.

**Answer: (A) only 16**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-26.title: Factor
kangaroo-at-2019-student-26.body:
$|n^2-2n-3| = |n-3|\cdot|n+1|$. A product of two non-negative integers is prime only if one factor is 1 and the other is prime.

- $|n-3|=1$: $n=4$ gives $1\cdot5=5$ ✓; $n=2$ gives $1\cdot3=3$ ✓.
- $|n+1|=1$: $n=0$ gives $3\cdot1=3$ ✓; $n=-2$ gives $5\cdot1=5$ ✓.

So there are **4** such integers.

**Answer: (D) 4**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-27.title: Diagonal by Pythagoras
kangaroo-at-2019-student-27.body:
$DE$ and $FB$ are both perpendicular to $EF$, so they are parallel. Going from $D$ to $B$ we move $5+2=7$ in the direction of $DE$ and $1$ perpendicular to it. So
$$DB=\sqrt{7^2+1^2}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2.$$
$DB$ is the diagonal of the square, so the side is $\frac{5\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=5$. This is not among (A)–(D).

**Answer: (E) another value**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-27.title: Watch the trap
kangaroo-at-2019-student-27.body:
(D) $5\sqrt2$ is the length of the **diagonal**, not the side. The side length is $5$, so (E).

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-29.title: Inclusion–exclusion
kangaroo-at-2019-student-29.body:
The centres form an equilateral triangle with side 2 (each centre lies on the other two circles). The grey zone is the part covered by exactly two circles.

- Each lens (intersection of two circles at distance 2 with radius 2) has area $2\left(\frac{\pi\cdot4}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot4\right) = \frac{8\pi}3-2\sqrt3$ (two circular segments of $120^\circ$).
- The part common to all three circles is the Reuleaux triangle on the three centres: area = triangle + three $60^\circ$ segments $=\sqrt3 + 3\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}-\sqrt3\right) = 2\pi-2\sqrt3$.

Each lens consists of a grey part and the common white part, so
$$\text{grey} = 3\left(\tfrac{8\pi}3-2\sqrt3\right) - 3\,(2\pi-2\sqrt3) = 2\pi.$$

**Answer: (D) $2\pi$**

kangaroo-at-2019-student-30.title: Small middle region
kangaroo-at-2019-student-30.body:
The whole grid sums to $5\cdot15=75$, so each section sums to $25$. The top-right section $U$ (6 cells) consists of the three cells of row 1 on the right, two cells of row 2 and the last cell of row 3; the bottom-left section $L$ is its mirror image; the middle section $M$ has 13 cells: 2, 3, 3, 3, 2 cells in rows 1 to 5.

The smallest possible sums of the parts of $M$ in the rows are $1+2=3$ for a 2-cell part and $1+2+3=6$ for a 3-cell part, together $3+6+6+6+3=24$. As $M$ sums to 25, every row part of $M$ is $\{1,2\}$ or $\{1,2,3\}$, except for exactly one row that has one more ($\{1,3\}$ or $\{1,2,4\}$). The same holds for columns.

In the typical case rows 1 and 2 are not exceptional: then the right part of row 1 is $\{3,4,5\}$ (sum 12) and the right part of row 2 is $\{4,5\}$ (sum 9), so the remaining cell of $U$ in row 3 is $25-12-9=4$. In the last column the $U$-part consists of the top cell, the row-2 cell and this 4, and it must sum to 12 or 11 (column version of the argument). The row-2 cell is 4 or 5 but not 4 (same column as the 4), so it is 5, and the top-right cell is $12-9=3$ or $11-9=2$; from row 1 it is in $\{3,4,5\}$, hence **3**. (Checking the exceptional cases leads to contradictions.)

A complete solution:
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}1&2&4&5&3\\3&1&2&4&5\\5&3&1&2&4\\4&5&3&1&2\\2&4&5&3&1\end{array}$$
Top-right section $4+5+3+4+5+4=25$, bottom-left section $5+4+5+2+4+5=25$, middle $25$.

**Answer: (C) 3**
